title: Meta Is the Only Big AI Spender With Nothing to Rent Back
subtitle: Capital spending is swallowing half of every sales dollar, leaving Meta with no cloud business to bail it out.
summary: Meta reports third-quarter earnings on October 21 as capital spending pushes past half of its revenue. While Big Tech peers lease excess data centers to paying clients, Meta must fund its entire computing buildout through digital ads and a fresh consumer subscription.

bodyHtml:
Every other cloud giant is building digital real estate to rent out to paying tenants. Meta is building a private power grid just to light its own digital billboard.

The Numbers That Matter
Price LIVE$709.33
Market Cap$1.81T
Forward P/E20.5x
Total Revenue (TTM)$228.25B
52-Week Low$520.26
52-Week High$779.82
Analyst ConsensusStrong Buy (58 analysts)
Analyst Target Mean$814.51
Price refreshes live · All other figures as of October 16, 2026

When you scroll Instagram, check WhatsApp, or tap through Facebook, you feed a single massive advertising engine. Ads generate roughly 98% of Meta’s top line, delivering $59.363 billion last quarter alone. Its only consumer side project is Muse, a new conversational agent launched in September with a free tier alongside $20 and $100 monthly subscriptions. Outside of that subscription experiment and smart glasses inside Reality Labs, Meta makes its money by showing you sponsored posts.

That distinction changes everything about how the AI buildout works. Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon can justify spending tens of billions on specialized chips because they lease that spare capacity back to corporate software clients. Meta has no commercial cloud business. Every transformer model, cluster of graphics processors, and gigawatt power purchase must pay for itself through its own consumer software. It is the only hyperscaler where the buildout carries no paying enterprise tenant to split the bill.

The pressure on the core business is already showing up in the plumbing. Last quarter, revenue jumped 28% to $60.801 billion, powered by a 14% increase in ad impressions and a 12% rise in average ad prices across 3.60 billion daily users. Yet operating income dropped 8% and operating margin shrank to 30.9% from 43.0% a year earlier. Total costs and expenses surged 55% to $42.026 billion, weighed down by $2.40 billion in legal charges and $1.18 billion in severance from trimming roughly 8,000 roles. Diluted earnings of $6.18 missed Wall Street expectations near $7.19 by a wide mark.

The real collision, however, is happening on the capital expenditure line. Chief Financial Officer Susan Li narrowed full-year capex guidance to between $130 billion and $145 billion, roughly double the $72.22 billion spent in 2025. Because Meta spent $50.92 billion in the first half, it must burn between $79 billion and $94 billion across the final six months. That requires spending roughly $40 billion to $47 billion every single quarter against Q2's $31.08 billion.

That official number does not even capture the full scope of the obligations. To ease the immediate cash hit, Meta is offloading infrastructure into complex lease structures. In El Paso, a joint venture with BlackRock will build a one-gigawatt site where Meta owns just 20%, but shoulders roughly $13 billion in residual value guarantees. Meanwhile, its Hyperion facility in Louisiana expanded to five gigawatts and over $50 billion of total investment. Factor in clean energy agreements with Vistra, TerraPower, and Oklo supporting up to 6.6 gigawatts by 2035, and commitments are exploding off the balance sheet. In the first quarter alone, multi-year cloud deals and infrastructure agreements triggered a $107 billion step-up in contractual obligations.

For equity investors, this shifts the entire math. The stock trades like a high-margin digital media monopoly, but the company is spending like a heavy industrial utility. For shares to re-rate higher, Meta either needs capital expenditures to visibly plateau or Muse must prove it can generate billions in standalone software revenue. Muse racked up 5 million downloads in 22 days according to Sensor Tower, outpacing early ChatGPT adoption, and The Information reports over 3 million weekly users and about 1 million daily prompters. Citigroup models more than $27 billion in annual Muse revenue by 2030, but Meta currently discloses zero revenue from the product.

Investors auditing the upcoming print must also dodge a glaring comparison trap. Third-quarter headlines will tout astronomical year-over-year earnings growth because the year-ago base sat at just $1.05 per share due to a one-time $15.93 billion tax charge. Strip out that non-cash hit, and normalized earnings were $7.25. Any headline reporting triple-digit profit acceleration is purely an accounting quirk.

The short thesis argues that Meta’s cash engine is being hollowed out long before AI yields an actual return. Free cash flow plunged 91% to just $784 million in the second quarter, leaving a paper-thin margin of 1.3% against a top line exceeding $60 billion. Reality Labs remains an open furnace, burning $4.619 billion in a single quarter while generating a meager $431 million in revenue. With second-half capital expenditures racing past $40 billion a quarter, full-year free cash flow is on track to flatline or turn negative.

Depreciation expense rose 46% to $6.356 billion last quarter, signaling that the accounting hangover from these data centers has barely begun. Capital spending may step up toward Guggenheim's 2027 projection of $225 billion. If Muse fails to become a separately disclosed revenue line by the fourth quarter, the thesis that Meta trapped itself in an unpayable capex treadmill becomes impossible to refute.

When Meta reports after the closing bell on October 21, the market will not care about another digital advertising beat. The only signal that counts is whether management offers a credible ceiling on 2027 spending and names a real dollar figure for AI.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in META. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
